title: Payment Is How the Owner Buys Certainty One Month at a Time
summary: Every construction payment is a trade: cash for verified work, clean title and a smaller unknown. This lesson walks the payment cycle from pay application to lender draw, and shows how the schedule of values, retainage and lien waivers each protect a different part of the owner's position.
body:
A construction payment is not a bill you settle. It is a monthly trade in which the owner exchanges cash for three things: verified work in place, clean title, and a contractor still able to finish.

Recall

Q. What is a hold point in an inspection and test plan?

A. A step the work may not pass until a named person has inspected and released it in writing. Work that covers a hold point without release is a nonconformance, whatever its quality.

Q. Why does title to stored materials matter before you pay for them?

A. Because paying for material that is not yet built in only protects you if the owner actually gets title, the material is insured, identified and stored where it can be inspected. Otherwise you have paid for something a failed supplier's creditors may claim.

Q. What is survey control on a site?

A. The fixed, checked reference points and benchmarks from which every line and level on the job is set out. If control is wrong, every element built from it is wrong in the same way.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, LEX sits beside me this week because payment is where cost control and law meet every single month. On a typical project you will approve somewhere around 20 to 30 payment cycles. Each one is a chance to keep money behind the work, or to let it drift ahead. The developer who pays carefully finishes with cash in hand and leverage over the closeout. The developer who pays loosely discovers, usually at the worst moment, that he has funded work that is not there, to a contractor who is not paying the trades, on a title that now carries claims.

The payment cycle in plain English

Once a month the contractor tells you how much work it believes it has done. Someone you trust checks that claim against the site. You agree a number, hold some of it back, collect evidence that the people below the contractor have been paid, and release the rest. If a lender funds the job, its draw follows the same rhythm a few days later.

The professional framing has five documents. The pay application is the contractor's formal request for payment for a period. In the United States the most common form is the American Institute of Architects pair: the G702 application and certificate for payment, and the G703 continuation sheet that lists every line. The schedule of values is the agreed breakdown of the contract sum into lines that each application bills against. The certificate is the architect's or owner's representative's statement of the amount properly due. Lien waivers are signed releases of the right to claim against your property for the amounts paid. And the draw request is your own package to the lender.

Here is a worked example with hypothetical round numbers. A 10,000,000 dollar contract. By the end of month 6 the contractor claims 4,000,000 dollars of work complete to date, including 200,000 dollars of stored steel. Your quantity surveyor walks the site and agrees 3,800,000 dollars, rejecting 200,000 dollars of drywall claimed on a floor where only framing is up. Retainage at 10 percent of 3,800,000 is 380,000 dollars, leaving 3,420,000 dollars earned less retainage. Previous certificates total 2,900,000 dollars. The payment due this month is 520,000 dollars, not the 700,000 dollars the contractor would have been paid on its own claim.

The schedule of values is the backbone

Every later argument about payment is decided by how the schedule of values was built. A schedule with eight lines, each worth over a million dollars, cannot be measured; your checker ends up guessing a percentage of a huge vague line. A schedule with 120 lines, split by trade, floor and area, can be measured almost by counting.

The risk to watch is front-loading: pricing early lines such as mobilisation, general conditions and site work above their true value, so the contractor collects cash ahead of the work. The control is to review the schedule of values before the first application as carefully as you reviewed the bid, compare each line with your own cost plan, and refuse to certify until the lines are realistic. Week 49 called the schedule of values a scope document. It is also a cash flow document, and the contractor knows that better than most owners.

Say that out loud now.

I pay for measured work against a schedule of values I approved, never for a percentage of a line I cannot measure.

Retainage and lien waivers protect different things

Retainage, called holdback in Canada, is a percentage of each payment kept back until completion. It has two jobs: it gives the owner money to finish defective or incomplete work if the contractor walks, and it gives the contractor a reason to come back for the punch list. Levels around 5 to 10 percent, often reduced at the halfway point, are common commercial practice, not a standard, and in many places statute caps or governs them; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Lien waivers protect title. A subcontractor who is not paid can often register a lien on your property, even though you paid the general contractor in full. Waivers come in four kinds: conditional or unconditional, and progress or final. A conditional waiver takes effect only when the stated payment clears. An unconditional waiver is effective on signing. The working rule is simple: collect conditional waivers with this month's application, and unconditional waivers for last month's payment, from the contractor and every significant subcontractor and supplier. A gap in last month's unconditional waivers is the single best early warning that money you paid is not reaching the trades.

Second worked example. The contractor delivers waivers this month from 9 of its 11 major subcontractors. The two missing are the electrical and mechanical trades, who together billed 600,000 dollars last month. You do not refuse to pay the whole application. You hold the 600,000 dollars, pay the rest, and require either the missing waivers or joint cheques to those two trades. That keeps the job moving while closing the one hole that matters.

How the best do it

Large owners and contractors run payment as a measured process with a fixed calendar. A pencil copy of the application arrives several days before the official one; owner, cost consultant and contractor walk the site together and agree the numbers before anything is signed; the official application then simply records what was agreed. Many top general contractors also track subcontractor payment and waiver status in the same system as the schedule. A small developer can copy all of this with a calendar, a one-page site walk sheet and a waiver log.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: retainage you owe is a liability your accountant must record correctly, and when costs are recognised for tax depends on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: every certificate you or your representative sign states that work is in place; a false certificate is a misrepresentation. Banking: the lender's monitor checks your certified amounts, so a disciplined owner gets faster draws. Governance: decide in writing who may approve a payment and what evidence they must see first. Estate: unpaid retainage and contingent lien claims are obligations an estate would inherit, so record them. Exit: a buyer or refinance lender will search title, and an unresolved lien delays both.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on the value of work in place; construction lawyer, on lien, retainage and payment terms where the project sits.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying for billing rather than for work: certifying the contractor's percentages, accepting stored materials without title and insurance, and accepting a waiver log with gaps. The control is an independent site measurement before every certificate, written conditions for stored materials, and a rule that no payment is released against a missing unconditional waiver for last month.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks retainage is his margin of safety and stops checking. Ten percent of what has been paid is small compared with an overbilled job, a re-procured trade and a set of liens. Retainage is the last line of defence, not the first.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught that the lender funds a finished building one verified slice at a time and tests every month that the money left will finish it. This lesson is the slice itself. The draw can only be as honest as the certificate under it, and the certificate can only be as honest as the schedule of values and the site walk under that.

Recap

Payment is a monthly trade of cash for verified work, clean title and a solvent contractor. The schedule of values decides whether work can be measured, retainage holds money back for completion, and lien waivers prove the money reached the trades. A disciplined cycle makes the lender's draw fast and the closeout yours to control.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: how the collapse of Carillion in 2018 exposed the payment chain.
checklist: I review the schedule of values line by line against my cost plan before the first application.
I require a pencil application and a joint site walk before the official one.
My quantity surveyor measures work in place; I do not certify the contractor's percentages.
I pay for stored materials only with title, insurance, identification and inspection access.
I collect conditional waivers this month and unconditional waivers for last month.
I keep a waiver log for the contractor and every major subcontractor and supplier.
I hold the specific amount affected by a missing waiver rather than freezing the whole application.
I know which statute governs retainage and liens where the project sits.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every construction payment is a trade. I give cash, and in return I get three things: verified work in place, clean title, and a contractor still able to finish. The contractor bills monthly against a schedule of values I approved before the first application, split finely enough to measure. My quantity surveyor walks the site and certifies what is really there, not what was billed. I hold back retainage, typically 5 to 10 percent as a commercial practice, so there is money to finish if the contractor walks and a reason to come back for the punch list. And I collect lien waivers: conditional for this month, unconditional for last month, from the contractor and every major trade. A gap in last month's waivers is my earliest warning that money is not reaching the trades. The lender's draw follows the same evidence. If my certificate is honest, the draw is fast, and the closeout stays mine to control.
terms: Pay application — the contractor's formal monthly request for payment, listing work complete and stored materials against each line of the schedule of values.
Retainage — a percentage of each payment held back until completion, called holdback in Canada, to secure finishing and correction of the work.
Lien waiver — a signed release of the right to claim against the property for amounts paid; conditional waivers take effect when payment clears, unconditional ones on signing.

hostile.q: You certified 3,800,000 dollars of work in place. Your contractor's electrical subcontractor says it has not been paid for two months. Why should I release this draw?
hostile.a: Because the draw does not include that risk. Last month's unconditional waivers from the electrical and mechanical trades were missing, so I held their 600,000 dollars and required joint cheques before it moves. The rest is supported by my quantity surveyor's measured walk, conditional waivers for this month and a clean title update. I will send you the waiver log and the hold calculation today.

title: Carillion 2018: When the Payment Chain Broke at the Top
summary: Carillion, a large British construction and services group, entered compulsory liquidation in January 2018 after a profit warning the summer before. Its collapse left subcontractors unpaid and their retention money stranded. Ford and Cole take the case through seven steps and draw one rule about where money owed down the chain should sit.
rule: Rule 117: Never let money owed to the trades, including retention and advance payments, sit unprotected with a party whose balance sheet you have not checked; pay against verified work and track that it reaches the people who did it.
body:
Carillion did not fail on one building. It failed because a long chain of payment terms let the company at the top hold other people's money, and when it went, that money went with it.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between a conditional and an unconditional lien waiver?

A. A conditional waiver releases lien rights only once the stated payment actually clears. An unconditional waiver releases them on signing, so it should only be collected for money already received.

Q. What is a nonconformance report?

A. A written record that work or material does not meet the specification, with the proposed disposition, such as repair, replace or accept with engineering approval, and who signed it off.

Q. What does an expediter do on long-lead procurement?

A. Tracks each critical order through the supplier's production, inspection and shipping, and escalates early when a date slips, so the schedule hears about a problem before the delivery is missed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this is a case about where money sits and what the accounts said about it. You will never run a company of Carillion's size. You will hire contractors who behave like it on a smaller scale: pay the trades slowly, hold their retention, and use their cash to fund the next job. The lesson travels down to a single building intact.

The public record I rely on here is the 2018 report of a joint inquiry by two committees of the United Kingdom House of Commons and contemporary reporting. I keep to facts I am confident of and leave out figures I cannot verify. Anything I describe as typical is commercial practice, not a finding.

1. Timeline

Carillion was a listed British group that built and maintained public and private infrastructure, including hospitals, roads and rail, and ran large facilities service contracts. In July 2017 it issued a profit warning, recognising a large write-down on a group of major contracts, and its share price fell sharply. Through the autumn it sought new financing and asset sales. On 15 January 2018 it entered compulsory liquidation. Work on projects including two major hospitals stopped, thousands of subcontractors and suppliers became unsecured creditors, and public bodies had to arrange for others to finish or run what Carillion had been doing.

2. Key decisions

Three kinds of decision mattered. The company bid for large fixed-price contracts at thin margins. It recognised revenue on troubled contracts in a way the later inquiry criticised as optimistic, so profits appeared before the cash that should have backed them. And it stretched the time it took to pay its supply chain, reportedly to as long as 120 days, while offering suppliers an early payment facility through banks, at a discount, if they wanted their money sooner.

3. Assumptions

The assumptions were that new contracts would keep generating cash, that problem contracts would recover, and that lenders and the supply chain would keep funding the gap. Subcontractors assumed a company of that size and with that client list could not simply stop. Many clients assumed that the main contractor's size was itself a form of security.

4. Incentives

Long payment terms improve a contractor's cash position at the expense of its suppliers. Early payment facilities let suppliers buy back their own money at a price. Management was rewarded on reported results. Public clients were under pressure to award to the lowest compliant bid. Every incentive pushed cash up the chain and risk down it.

Say that out loud now.

Long payment terms are a loan from the trades to the contractor, and the trades did not get a vote.

5. Warning signs ignored

Slow payment to the supply chain was widely known in the industry before the collapse. The profit warning of July 2017 showed that reported profit on major contracts had not been real. Rapid moves to raise cash and sell assets followed. For an owner, the specific signs are the ones you can see from your own job: subcontractors complaining about late payment, requests to reduce retention early, pressure to approve applications before the site walk, and a contractor offering to pay its trades faster if you pay it sooner.

6. Point of no return

For the company, it was the point at which new financing could no longer be raised, in the weeks before January 2018. For an owner with a job under way, the point of no return came earlier and was quieter: the last month in which money owed to the trades, including retention, could have been moved out of the contractor's hands by joint cheques, direct payment provisions or a retention held separately, before the insolvency froze it.

7. Root cause

The root cause, put simply, was a business model that funded itself with other people's money and reported profit before the cash arrived. The insolvency then did what insolvencies do: everyone owed money, including subcontractors whose retention had been held by Carillion, joined the queue of unsecured creditors.

Cole's view: retention and the accounts

Mr Shabazz, the audit lesson is that reported profit on a construction contract is an estimate, built on assumed cost to complete and assumed recoveries on claims. When those assumptions drift, profit can be overstated for years before a write-down catches up. Read any contractor's accounts with three questions: how much revenue is recognised but not yet billed, how much rests on unagreed claims, and how fast is the cash conversion compared with reported profit. If profit is high and cash is weak, ask why.

On retention, in many legal systems money held back from a subcontractor is simply a debt owed by the contractor; if the contractor fails, the subcontractor is an ordinary creditor. Some jurisdictions require retention or holdback to be held in trust or a separate account; others do not. Which applies where your project sits is a legal question [unverified — confirm independently]. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer licensed where the project sits.

What an owner can do on one building

This is a worked example with hypothetical round numbers. Your contractor holds 10 percent retention from its subcontractors on a 20,000,000 dollar job; at 60 percent complete that is roughly 1,200,000 dollars of the trades' money sitting with the contractor. You hold your own 10 percent from the contractor. If the contractor fails, your retention helps you finish, but the subcontractors' retention is gone unless the contract or the law protects it. Three controls: require the contractor's subcontract retention to be held in a separate account or released as each trade finishes; reserve the right to pay trades directly or by joint cheque on missing waivers; and check the contractor's accounts and bonding before award and at least yearly.

A second worked example shows why the bond question belongs at award. A payment bond on that 20,000,000 dollar contract might cost a premium in the range of a percent or so of the contract sum, as commercial practice that varies with the contractor's credit, not a standard. That premium buys a surety whose business is paying unpaid trades if the contractor cannot. Compare it with the cost of curing liens, re-procuring trades and delay on a half-built job, and it is often cheap. Decide with numbers, not habit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a contractor's size as its solvency. The control is a financial review at award and annually, payment bonds where available and economic, and a contract that lets you see and protect payment to the trades.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks subcontractor payment is the contractor's problem. Then the liens land on his title, and the trades he needs to finish the job will not return without being paid twice.

Callback

In Week 72, REGA and Cole taught integrity checks on the people you deal with: source of funds, beneficial ownership and reputation. Contractor financial due diligence is the same discipline applied to capacity rather than character. A contractor can be honest and still be unable to pay.

Recap

Carillion collapsed in January 2018 after a July 2017 profit warning, leaving its supply chain as unsecured creditors. Long payment terms and held retention had made the trades its lenders. Rule 117 keeps money owed down the chain verified, traced and out of the hands of a party whose balance sheet you have not checked.

Next: Priya on The Money: what retainage, waivers and draw timing do to your cash and your returns.
checklist: I review the contractor's accounts for unbilled revenue, unagreed claims and cash conversion before award.
I repeat the financial review at least once a year on long jobs.
I ask how the contractor holds subcontractor retention and whether law requires it in trust.
My contract lets me pay trades directly or by joint cheque if waivers are missing.
I track complaints of slow payment from subcontractors as an early warning.
I refuse requests to reduce retention early while work is unfinished.
I consider payment and performance bonds at award and price them as a real option.
I never approve an application before the site walk to help a contractor's cash flow.
head: Field checklist
speak: Carillion was a large British construction and services group. In July 2017 it issued a profit warning on a group of major contracts, and on 15 January 2018 it entered compulsory liquidation. Hospitals and other projects stopped, and thousands of subcontractors became unsecured creditors, including those whose retention money Carillion was holding. The inquiry that followed criticised optimistic revenue recognition and very long payment terms to the supply chain. The root cause was a model that funded itself with other people's money and reported profit before the cash arrived. On a single building, the same pattern appears as slow payment to the trades, pressure to reduce retention and requests to pay before the site walk. Rule 117: never let money owed to the trades, including retention, sit unprotected with a party whose balance sheet you have not checked; pay against verified work and track that it reaches the people who did it.
terms: Unsecured creditor — a person owed money who holds no security over specific assets, and so ranks behind secured lenders in an insolvency.
Early payment facility — an arrangement, often run through banks, that lets a supplier receive payment before the due date in exchange for a discount.
Joint cheque — a payment made out jointly to the contractor and a named subcontractor, so the money cannot be released without both.

hostile.q: Your contractor is twice the size of you. Why are you asking for its accounts and telling it how to hold its subcontractors' retention?
hostile.a: Because size is not solvency, and if you fail, your subcontractors' liens land on my title and my lender's draw stops. I am not asking for anything unusual: accounts at award and yearly, retention held so the trades are protected, and a right to pay trades directly if waivers go missing. If your finances are as strong as you say, none of that will cost you anything.

title: What Retainage, Waivers and Draw Timing Do to Your Cash and Your Returns
summary: The payment process moves real money and real time. Retainage is cash the contractor finances, draw lag is a gap the owner finances, and a missing waiver can delay a draw. This lesson prices each and shows what they do to interest carry, equity and the return.
body:
Payment terms are financing terms in disguise: retainage is a loan from the contractor to you, draw lag is a loan from you to the job, and both show up in interest, equity and the return.

Recall

Q. What is a schedule of values?

A. The agreed breakdown of the contract sum into lines that each monthly pay application bills against. Fine lines can be measured; coarse ones invite guessing and front-loading.

Q. What is a mock-up, and when is it worth its cost?

A. A full-size sample of an assembly, built and tested before production work, to agree quality and detailing. It is worth its cost wherever a defect would be repeated many times or is hard to fix later, such as a facade or wet area.

Q. What is dewatering?

A. Lowering groundwater temporarily so excavation and foundations can be built in the dry, by pumping from sumps or wells, with effects on neighbours and discharge permits that must be managed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most developers model cost, interest and timing, but treat payment mechanics as administration. They are not. On a 20,000,000 dollar contract, the difference between a disciplined payment process and a loose one can be several hundred thousand dollars of interest, a delayed draw that forces you to fund trades from your own pocket, and a closeout in which the contractor holds the leverage. Today we price it.

Retainage is contractor-financed cash

Every dollar of retainage you hold is a dollar of work you have received and not yet paid for. That is a loan from the contractor to you, interest free in the contract, but priced into the bid. Contractors who expect heavy retainage, or who expect it to be released slowly, add a premium. The professional framing is that retainage has a benefit, security and leverage, and a cost, higher bid prices and lower contractor working capital.

Worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A 20,000,000 dollar contract over 20 months, billed evenly at 1,000,000 dollars a month. Retainage is 10 percent until 50 percent complete, then no further retention on later billings. At the halfway point you are holding 1,000,000 dollars, and that balance stays until completion. On average across the job you hold about 750,000 dollars. If your construction loan costs 7 percent a year, holding that cash rather than drawing it saves interest of roughly 52,500 dollars a year, or about 87,500 dollars over 20 months. If the contractor adds even half a percent to its price for the retention terms, that is 100,000 dollars, and the interest saving is gone. The point is not the exact figure. The point is that retention is a priced term, and you should decide it with the bid, not by habit.

Say that out loud now.

Retainage is security I pay for in the bid price, so I set it deliberately and release it on a schedule I can defend.

Draw lag is owner-financed cash

The contractor's payment terms run from its application. Your lender's draw runs from your request, after its monitor's inspection and a title update. If the contract says you pay 30 days after the application and the lender typically funds 10 to 15 days after a complete request, there is little gap. If your request is late, incomplete or missing a waiver, the lender holds the draw and the contractor still expects payment.

Second worked example. The monthly certificate is 1,000,000 dollars. The draw is delayed 20 days because two unconditional waivers are missing. To keep the trades working you fund the payment from equity and wait for the draw. That is 1,000,000 dollars of equity out for 20 days. If your equity's target return is 18 percent a year, the opportunity cost is about 10,000 dollars for that one month. Repeat it four times on a job and it is a real number, and worse, it trains your contractor to expect you to bridge their cash flow.

What the payment process does to the return

Three effects reach the internal rate of return, the annual return that makes the present value of all the project's cash flows zero. First, timing: cash going out earlier lowers the return, so overbilling and early retention release hurt it twice, once in interest and once in timing. Second, leakage: money paid for work not in place, or paid twice to cure a lien, is cost with no value. Third, delay: a draw held for paperwork can slow trades, and delay compounds through carry and lease-up.

A rule of thumb many cost managers use, as practitioner habit rather than a standard, is to run the cash flow monthly from the schedule of values, not from a smooth curve, and to treat any month where billed value runs more than a few percent ahead of measured value as a cost-control issue, not just a payment one.

Third worked example. Suppose the contractor overbills by 500,000 dollars and the overbilling sits uncorrected for 6 months. At a 7 percent loan rate, that is roughly 17,500 dollars of interest on money paid for work that did not exist. The bigger cost is risk: if the contractor fails in month 6, the 500,000 dollars is not a timing difference any more. It is a loss you fund to finish, and your retainage was sized against the work, not against the overbilling.

Lien exposure is a contingent cost

A lien is not money you owe until someone proves it, but it is money a buyer, lender or title insurer will make you deal with. On a sale or refinance, title must usually be clear, and a lien is typically bonded off, paid or discharged before closing. That costs time, a bond premium and legal fees, even when the claim is weak. Hold a small reserve against disputed payments to the trades, and treat each unresolved waiver as a contingent liability in your monthly report.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On a personal balance sheet, Mr Shabazz, payment discipline shows up in two lines. One is liquidity: every time you bridge a held draw from your own resources, your personal liquidity floor drops, and Week 7 taught that the floor is what lets you say no. The other is contingent liability: if you have guaranteed the construction loan, every unresolved lien or overbilled month increases the chance that guarantee is called. A clean payment process is one of the cheapest ways to protect your own net worth. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor, on work in place and the cash flow forecast; construction lawyer, on retention and payment terms; your lender's counsel, on the draw conditions.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting payment mechanics run on autopilot until a held draw forces you to fund the job from equity. The control is a monthly cash flow built from the schedule of values, a draw calendar agreed with the lender, and a waiver log closed before each request goes in.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sets retainage by copying the last job and never asks what it costs. Then he negotiates it down under pressure late in the job, giving away his leverage for nothing in return.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage showed that the internal rate of return punishes early cash out and rewards late cash out, and that small timing changes move it more than people expect. Payment terms are where that sensitivity lives on a construction job: overbilling, early retention release and bridged draws are all early cash out.

Recap

Retainage is security paid for in the bid, draw lag is a gap the owner finances, and liens are contingent costs that surface at sale or refinance. Model payment monthly from the schedule of values, keep the waiver log closed, and set retention as a priced term.

Next: LEX on The Rules: liens, waivers, holdbacks and prompt payment, and how the law moves money down the chain.
checklist: I build the monthly cash flow from the schedule of values, not a smooth curve.
I set retainage with the bid and price its effect on the contract sum.
I agree a draw calendar with the lender before the first request.
I close the waiver log before each draw request goes in.
I flag any month where billed value runs ahead of measured value.
I hold a small reserve against disputed payments to trades.
I report unresolved liens and waivers as contingent liabilities every month.
I never release retention early without receiving something of value in return.
head: Field checklist
speak: Payment terms are financing terms in disguise. Retainage is a loan from the contractor to me: on a 20,000,000 dollar job with 10 percent held to the halfway point, I hold about 1,000,000 dollars at peak, which saves interest but is priced into the bid. So I set retention deliberately, with the bid. Draw lag is a loan from me to the job: if a draw is held for missing waivers, I either stop the trades or fund them from equity, and that costs me return and trains the contractor to expect it. The internal rate of return feels all of this, because overbilling and early release push cash out early, and leakage and liens are cost with no value. So I build the monthly cash flow from the schedule of values, agree a draw calendar with the lender, close the waiver log before every request, and treat each unresolved lien as a contingent liability.
terms: Draw lag — the time between paying the contractor and receiving the lender's draw that funds that payment.
Contingent liability — an obligation that may arise depending on a future event, such as a lien claim being proved.
Internal rate of return — the annual return that makes the present value of all a project's cash flows equal zero.

hostile.q: Your draw is 20 days late again because of missing paperwork. Are you funding the contractor from your own pocket, and how long can you keep doing it?
hostile.a: This month I funded one payment of 1,000,000 dollars from equity for 20 days, and I have stopped doing it. From next month the waiver log must be closed five working days before the request, the contractor's application is due earlier to match, and any trade without a waiver is paid by joint cheque. I will send you the revised draw calendar this week.

title: Liens, Waivers, Holdbacks and Prompt Payment: How the Law Moves Money Down the Chain
summary: Construction payment is governed by two layers: the contract between the parties, and statutes that give unpaid trades rights against the property and, in some places, set payment deadlines. This lesson explains lien rights, waivers, pay-when-paid clauses and prompt payment rules as concepts, with a Two Systems comparison of Canada and Guyana.
body:
The contract says who pays whom and when, but in most places statute then reaches past the contract and gives unpaid trades a claim against your land; an owner who reads only the contract misses half the rules.

Recall

Q. What is retainage, and what are its two jobs?

A. A percentage of each payment held back until completion. It secures money to finish or correct the work if the contractor walks, and gives the contractor a reason to return for the punch list.

Q. What is a special inspection?

A. An inspection of specified critical work, such as structural welding, high-strength bolting or concrete placement, by a qualified independent inspector, required by the building code in addition to the building official's own inspections.

Q. In earthworks, what does compaction testing prove?

A. That fill has been placed and compacted to the density the engineer specified, layer by layer, usually by field density tests compared with a laboratory reference.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Quincy taught the mechanics this week. My job is to tell you which of them have legal teeth. Construction payment law exists because the trades at the bottom of the chain add value to your land but contract with someone else. Most legal systems decide that they should have some protection against an owner who has been enriched by their work. How much protection, and what you must do to stay clear of it, varies widely. I will teach the concepts. The conclusions for your project belong to a lawyer licensed where it sits.

Lien rights: a claim against the land

In the United States, mechanic's lien rights are created by state statute, and every state's statute is different. In broad terms, a contractor, subcontractor or supplier who improved the property and was not paid may record a lien against the property within a set period after its last work, and then enforce it by suit, which can end in a sale of the property to satisfy the debt. Many states require lower-tier claimants to serve a preliminary notice early in the job to preserve their rights, and many limit an owner's total exposure in some way. The deadlines, notice requirements and limits are state specific [unverified — confirm independently].

The practical consequence is that paying your general contractor in full does not, by itself, protect your land. If the general contractor does not pay a subcontractor, that subcontractor may still have a lien. That is why owners collect waivers, why title insurers ask about unpaid work before insuring a sale or loan, and why lenders want lien waivers with every draw.

Waivers: forms, timing and traps

Several states prescribe statutory waiver forms and treat a non-conforming waiver as ineffective. A few treat certain waivers signed before payment as unenforceable. Some forbid waiving lien rights in advance in the contract itself. So a waiver form copied from another state, or a clause that says the subcontractor waives all lien rights at signing, may protect you less than you think [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example in concept. Your contract includes a clause by which every subcontractor waives its lien rights at the start of the job. In some states that clause would be void as against public policy, leaving the subcontractor's full rights in place; in others it might be enforced. You do not want to discover which applies after a lien is recorded. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer licensed in the state where the project sits.

Say that out loud now.

The contract governs the parties; the lien statute governs my land; I need both read by a lawyer where the land is.

Pay-when-paid, pay-if-paid and prompt payment

Subcontracts often tie the subcontractor's payment to the contractor's. A pay-when-paid clause is usually read as fixing the timing of payment: the contractor pays once the owner pays, or within a reasonable time if the owner never does. A pay-if-paid clause tries to make owner payment a condition precedent, so that if the owner never pays, the subcontractor never gets paid. Courts in different states treat these differently, and some states refuse to enforce pay-if-paid at all, or preserve lien rights regardless [unverified — confirm independently].

Prompt payment statutes set deadlines for paying contractors and subcontractors and, often, interest on late payment. For federal government work in the United States, the federal Prompt Payment Act governs; many states have their own acts for public work, private work or both. Some statutes also limit retainage or require it to be released within a set time after completion. Whether your private project is covered, and what the deadlines are, is a question for counsel; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Some states also have trust fund statutes, which treat money paid to a contractor for a project as held in trust for the trades on that project, sometimes with personal liability for those who divert it. Ask your lawyer whether one applies [unverified — confirm independently].

Public land and payment bonds

On public projects in the United States, liens generally cannot attach to government property, so the law substitutes a bond. For federal construction, the Miller Act requires contractors above a threshold to provide a performance bond and a payment bond, and most states have similar statutes for state and local work, often called little Miller Acts. An unpaid subcontractor then claims against the surety rather than the land, again within strict notice periods. On a private project you can choose the same protection by requiring payment bonds in the contract. The threshold amounts and notice periods must be checked in the current statute; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

These are conceptual comparisons only; verify against primary source before you rely on any of it.

Canada. Construction liens and the statutory holdback are matters of provincial law, so each province has its own act. The general model is that the owner must hold back a statutory percentage of what is paid, that liens must be preserved within strict time limits, and that an owner who holds the correct holdback limits its exposure to lien claimants. Several provinces have added prompt payment timelines and fast adjudication of payment disputes in recent years, and federal legislation sets prompt payment rules for federal construction work. The percentages, time limits and which provinces have adopted which reforms must be confirmed in the current statute [unverified — confirm independently].

Guyana. Guyana has a common law based legal system. I am not able to confirm whether it has a construction-specific lien and holdback statute comparable to the Canadian provincial acts, or prompt payment legislation [unverified — confirm independently]. Where no such statute exists, an unpaid trade's remedies would rest mainly on its contract and general law, which shifts weight onto the contract itself: payment terms, security, retention held separately and direct payment rights. Professional sign-off required: an attorney-at-law admitted in Guyana.

The lesson across both systems is the same: find out, before award, what statute adds to your contract, then write the contract so the two fit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming the contract is the whole of the law. The control is a short written memo from local counsel before award covering lien rights and deadlines, waiver forms, enforceability of pay-if-paid and advance waivers, retention limits, prompt payment rules and any trust fund obligations.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner uses one waiver form on every project in every state, because it worked last time. A non-statutory form in a statutory state can be worthless exactly when you need it.

Callback

In Week 30, I taught that title is the bundle of rights a buyer or lender actually gets, and that encumbrances recorded against it travel with the land. A construction lien is exactly that kind of encumbrance, created by someone you never signed a contract with. Payment discipline is title protection.

Recap

Payment is governed by the contract and by statute. Lien rights let unpaid trades claim against the land, waivers must meet local form and timing rules, pay-if-paid clauses are treated differently by different courts, and prompt payment and trust fund statutes may add deadlines and duties. Get a local memo before award.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: a full pay application worked line by line, from schedule of values to lender draw.
checklist: I get a written memo from local counsel on payment law before award.
I confirm lien deadlines, preliminary notice rules and any owner exposure limits.
I use statutory waiver forms where the state prescribes them.
I do not rely on advance lien waivers in the contract without counsel's view.
I know whether pay-when-paid or pay-if-paid is enforceable where the project sits.
I confirm whether prompt payment or retention release deadlines apply to private work.
I ask whether a trust fund statute applies to project money.
I treat any foreign or unfamiliar jurisdiction as unverified until local counsel confirms.
head: Field checklist
speak: Construction payment runs on two layers of rules. The contract says who pays whom and when. Statute then reaches past it. In the United States, each state's mechanic's lien law lets an unpaid contractor, subcontractor or supplier claim against the land itself, within strict deadlines, often after a preliminary notice. So paying my general contractor in full does not protect my title on its own. Waivers have to meet local form and timing rules, and some states refuse to enforce lien waivers signed in advance. Courts treat pay-when-paid and pay-if-paid clauses differently. Prompt payment acts may set deadlines and interest, and some states treat project money as held in trust for the trades. In Canada, liens and holdback are provincial, with recent prompt payment reforms in several provinces. For Guyana, I would need local counsel to confirm the position. Before award, I get a short written memo from a lawyer licensed where the land is.
terms: Mechanic's lien — a statutory claim against improved property by an unpaid contractor, subcontractor or supplier, enforceable against the land itself.
Pay-if-paid clause — a subcontract term that tries to make the owner's payment a condition of the subcontractor being paid at all.
Prompt payment statute — a law setting deadlines for paying contractors and subcontractors, often with interest on late payment.

hostile.q: Your contract has every subcontractor waive lien rights at signing. Our title insurer still wants waivers with every draw. Why should we pay for that paperwork?
hostile.a: Because in many places an advance waiver in the contract is not enforceable, and I would rather not test that after a lien is recorded. My counsel's memo for this jurisdiction says the statutory progress waivers are what protect title here, so we collect them every month and the insurer can rely on them. The cost is administration. The alternative is a lien that delays your closing.

title: A Pay Application Worked Line by Line, From Schedule of Values to Lender Draw
summary: This lesson works a full hypothetical pay application: measuring lines, stored materials, retainage with a step-down, previous certificates and the amount due. It then turns the certificate into a lender draw request and runs the in-balance check that decides whether the draw is released.
body:
A pay application is arithmetic you can check in ten minutes, and that is exactly why you should never sign one you have not checked.

Recall

Q. What does a pay-if-paid clause try to do?

A. Make the owner's payment a condition of the subcontractor being paid at all, so if the owner never pays, the subcontractor never does. Its enforceability varies by jurisdiction.

Q. What are Incoterms, in one sentence?

A. Standard trade terms published by the International Chamber of Commerce that set where risk and cost pass from seller to buyer in a delivery, such as at the seller's premises or at the destination.

Q. What is a logistics plan on a construction site?

A. A drawn plan showing access, cranes, hoists, laydown, deliveries, temporary services and traffic routes over time, so the site can actually be built in the sequence planned.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every month someone will hand you a page of numbers and ask for a signature. This lesson teaches you to read that page as a quantity surveyor does: line by line, with units, checking each step against the one before. All numbers are hypothetical and round. The retention terms used are commercial practice for illustration, not a standard.

Step 1: the schedule of values and what is claimed

The contract sum is 12,000,000 dollars. For clarity, we use six lines, though a real schedule would have many more. The contractor's month 8 application claims work complete to date on each line:

LineValue, dollarsClaimed to date, dollarsMeasured to date, dollars
General conditions1,200,000600,000480,000
Foundations1,800,0001,800,0001,800,000
Structure3,600,0002,700,0002,520,000
Envelope2,400,000600,000480,000
Mechanical, electrical and plumbing2,400,000500,000500,000
Finishes600,00000

Claimed work to date totals 6,200,000 dollars. Our measured total is 5,780,000 dollars. The differences have reasons. General conditions are time-related: 8 months of a 20 month schedule is 40 percent, so 480,000 dollars, not 600,000. Structure: the contractor claims 75 percent; we count 7 of 10 floors cast, 70 percent, 2,520,000 dollars. Envelope: we count 20 percent of the facade panels installed, 480,000 dollars.

Step 2: stored materials

The contractor also claims 300,000 dollars of curtain wall units stored at a bonded warehouse off site. Our contract allows payment for off-site stored materials only with a bill of sale transferring title, insurance naming the owner, units identified by tag, and an inspection. Three of the four conditions are met; the bill of sale is missing. We allow 0 this month and will allow 300,000 dollars next month once title is transferred. Week 115 explained why title comes first.

Total completed and stored to date, as certified: 5,780,000 dollars. Write that number on the page in your own hand before you look at anything else the contractor has calculated, because every later step depends on it and an error here flows through to retainage, the payment and the draw.

Step 3: retainage with a step-down

The contract holds 10 percent retainage until 50 percent of the contract sum is complete, then holds nothing further on later work, keeping what was already held. Fifty percent of 12,000,000 is 6,000,000 dollars. Our certified total, 5,780,000, is below that, so retainage is still 10 percent of everything: 578,000 dollars.

Earned less retainage: 5,780,000 minus 578,000 equals 5,202,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Measured work, less retainage, less what I have already certified, equals what I pay. Nothing else goes in that box.

Step 4: previous certificates and the amount due

Previous certificates, months 1 to 7, total 4,500,000 dollars. Current payment due: 5,202,000 minus 4,500,000 equals 702,000 dollars. On the contractor's own claim it would have been 6,200,000 less 620,000 retainage, 5,580,000, less 4,500,000, which is 1,080,000 dollars. The site walk moved 378,000 dollars of payment into later months, where it belongs.

Check the arithmetic both ways. Balance to finish plus retainage: contract sum 12,000,000 less earned less retainage 5,202,000 equals 6,798,000 dollars. That should equal remaining work, 12,000,000 less 5,780,000, which is 6,220,000, plus retainage held, 578,000, giving 6,798,000. It does. If it does not, there is an error on the page.

Step 5: waivers and holds

Last month's unconditional waivers are in from every trade except the envelope subcontractor, who was paid 150,000 dollars last month. We release 552,000 dollars now and 150,000 dollars when the waiver arrives, or by joint cheque. Total certified stays 702,000.

Step 6: the lender draw and the in-balance check

Our draw request this month: hard cost 702,000 dollars, soft costs of 98,000 dollars for design, testing and permits, and interest of 200,000 dollars funded from the interest reserve. Total draw: 1,000,000 dollars.

The lender tests balance. The total project budget is 22,500,000 dollars, funded by 7,000,000 dollars of equity, already spent first, and a 15,500,000 dollar loan. Before this request, 7,000,000 dollars of the loan has been drawn, so 8,500,000 dollars is undisbursed. Our independent cost to complete, measured from today and including this month's draw, has four parts. Remaining hard cost is the contract sum less previous certificates: 12,000,000 minus 4,500,000, which is 7,500,000 dollars, and that already includes this month's 702,000 and the retainage still to be released. Remaining soft costs are 250,000 dollars. Interest to completion, including this month's, is 500,000 dollars. Remaining contingency is 150,000 dollars. Total cost to complete: 8,400,000 dollars. Undisbursed loan of 8,500,000 against cost to complete of 8,400,000: in balance by 100,000 dollars, which is thin. A cushion that small means one bad month puts the loan out of balance, and we report it to the lender now, not later.

Step 7: next month, when the step-down bites

In month 9 the contractor transfers title to the curtain wall, and we measure total completed and stored to date at 6,800,000 dollars, including that 300,000. That is above the 6,000,000 dollar halfway mark, so the step-down applies. Retainage is 10 percent of the first 6,000,000 dollars, which is 600,000, and nothing on the 800,000 above it. Earned less retainage: 6,800,000 minus 600,000 equals 6,200,000 dollars. Previous certificates are now 4,500,000 plus 702,000, which is 5,202,000. Payment due: 6,200,000 minus 5,202,000 equals 998,000 dollars.

Notice what happened. This month's measured work was 1,020,000 dollars, and the payment is 998,000. Retainage rose by only 22,000 dollars, from 578,000 to 600,000. After the step-down almost every dollar of new work is paid in full, which is good for the contractor's cash and is exactly why the step-down should be triggered by measured progress, never by a request. It also means your leverage now rests on a fixed 600,000 dollars, so the quality of your measurement matters more in the second half of the job, not less. Keep every figure in dollars and every quantity in its own unit, floors, panels or months, so each line can be traced back to the site.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor, on measured work and cost to complete; lender's monitor, on its own inspection; construction lawyer, on stored material title.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing the contractor's totals because the arithmetic adds up. Arithmetic can be perfect on wrong quantities. The control is measuring each line, applying stored material conditions strictly and running the two-way check before signing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reports the loan in balance on budget remaining rather than on an independent cost to complete. A thin cushion then disappears in one month and the lender finds it first.

Callback

In Week 51, Quincy and Nadia taught earned value: comparing what you planned, what you spent and what the work is actually worth. A pay application is earned value applied to cash. The measured column is earned value; the claimed column is the contractor's hope.

Recap

Measure each line, apply stored material conditions, compute retainage on the certified total, subtract previous certificates, check the arithmetic both ways, hold for missing waivers, then build the draw and test balance on an independent cost to complete.

Next: Quincy on The Room: the pay application meeting when the contractor has overbilled.
checklist: I measure each line independently before looking at the contractor's percentage.
I price time-related lines by elapsed time, not by claim.
I apply every stored materials condition, including title, before paying.
I compute retainage on the certified total and apply the step-down exactly as written.
I subtract previous certificates and run the two-way balance check.
I hold specific amounts for missing waivers rather than the whole payment.
I test the loan's balance on an independent cost to complete.
I report a thin balance cushion to the lender before it becomes a shortfall.
head: Field checklist
speak: A pay application is arithmetic I can check in ten minutes. In this hypothetical, a 12,000,000 dollar contract, the contractor claimed 6,200,000 dollars of work to date. We measured 5,780,000: general conditions by elapsed time, structure by floors cast, envelope by panels installed. Stored curtain wall was refused for one month because title had not transferred. Retainage at 10 percent of the certified total was 578,000 dollars, so earned less retainage was 5,202,000. Less previous certificates of 4,500,000, the payment due was 702,000 dollars, not the 1,080,000 the contractor's own claim implied. I checked the arithmetic both ways, held 150,000 dollars for one missing waiver, and built the draw with soft costs and interest. Then I tested balance: undisbursed loan of 8,500,000 against an independent cost to complete of 8,400,000. That is in balance, but thin, so I tell the lender now.
terms: Stored materials — materials delivered but not yet built in, paid for only under conditions such as transfer of title, insurance and inspection.
Step-down — a contract term that reduces or stops further retainage once a set percentage of the work is complete.
Balance to finish — the contract sum less the amount earned less retainage, which should equal the remaining work plus retainage held.

hostile.q: Your certificate is 378,000 dollars below our application. You are starving our cash flow. On what basis?
hostile.a: On measurement. General conditions are billed by elapsed time, 8 of 20 months. Structure is 7 of 10 floors cast, envelope 20 percent of panels in place. The curtain wall in storage will be paid as soon as the bill of sale transfers title. I will walk the site with your team before next month's pencil application so we agree the numbers before either of us signs.

title: The Pay Application Meeting When the Contractor Has Overbilled
summary: A realistic monthly payment meeting in which the owner's measurement is well below the contractor's application and the contractor's project manager pushes hard. The lesson gives the lines to say and never to say, the question behind the question, and how to hold position without damaging the job.
body:
The payment meeting is not a negotiation about money; it is a disagreement about facts, and you win it by keeping it about facts.

Recall

Q. In the worked pay application, why were general conditions certified at 480,000 dollars rather than the 600,000 claimed?

A. Because general conditions are time-related. Eight months of a 20-month schedule is 40 percent of the 1,200,000 dollar line, which is 480,000.

Q. What is a witness point, as distinct from a hold point?

A. A step at which the inspector must be notified and may attend, but work may proceed if they do not come. A hold point stops the work until written release.

Q. What is a factory acceptance test?

A. A test of equipment at the manufacturer's works, before shipping, witnessed by the buyer or its representative, to confirm it meets the specification while defects are still cheap to fix.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will sit in this meeting every month. Most months it is routine. The month it is not, the contractor is usually short of cash, and the person across the table is under pressure from their own management. How you handle that meeting decides whether the money stays behind the work and whether the relationship survives. This is a scene, with hypothetical people and numbers.

The setting

Month 10 of a 20-month job. Around the table: you; your quantity surveyor; the lender's monitor, invited as an observer; and the contractor's project manager and commercial manager. The application claims 1,400,000 dollars this month. Your quantity surveyor's measured figure is 950,000 dollars. The contractor has also asked to reduce retainage to 5 percent now rather than at completion, and two subcontractors' waivers are missing.

The opening

Open with the bottom line and the basis, then stop. "Thank you for coming. Our certificate this month is 950,000 dollars. The difference from your application is on three lines, and we have the measurement for each. I'd like to go through them line by line, then talk about the retainage request and the two waivers."

Then wait. The contractor's project manager will push. "That's 450,000 short. We can't run the job on that. Our subs are already complaining."

The line to say: "I understand the pressure. Let's look at the lines, because if our measurement is wrong I want to fix it today." That keeps it about facts and gives them a fair route to more money: proving the work is there.

Say that out loud now.

If our measurement is wrong, I want to fix it today. If it is right, it stands.

The lines never to say

Never say "Fine, we'll sort it out next month." That converts an overbilling into a loan. Never say "Your company always does this." That turns a fact into a character attack and the meeting into a fight. Never say "The bank won't let me pay more." It may be true, but it hands your authority to the lender and invites the contractor to lobby the bank. And never sign any part of the certificate in the meeting before the measurement is agreed or the dispute is recorded.

The question behind the question

When a contractor overbills hard and asks for early retention release in the same meeting, the question behind the question is usually: can you help us with our cash? That is important information. It may mean a loss on this job, losses elsewhere, or a lender of their own tightening.

So ask, calmly: "Is there a cash flow issue on this job or across the business I should know about? If there is, it is better we plan for it together now than discover it through the subcontractors." Then stay silent. Let the silence do the work. Whatever they say goes in your notes and into your risk register.

The retainage request and the waivers

"On retainage, the contract holds it to completion. I'm not in a position to reduce it at this stage. If there is a specific proposal that gives the project something in return, such as a bond, put it in writing and we will consider it." That is a no that leaves a door open on terms.

"On the two waivers: we will pay the rest of the certificate on the normal date. The amounts for those two trades will be paid by joint cheque, or released when the waivers arrive." State it as process, not punishment.

Holding your state

The contractor may raise its voice. Keep yours slower and lower than theirs; pace and pause, from Week 5, are more persuasive than volume. Keep your hands still and your notes in front of you. If the meeting stops being about facts, end it: "Let's take a break. My quantity surveyor will walk the three lines with your team this afternoon, and we'll reconvene tomorrow at nine." Ending a meeting is not losing it.

A worked example of resolution: the afternoon walk finds 120,000 dollars of structure the measurement missed on a floor that was cast after the survey. The certificate moves to 1,070,000 dollars. You thank them for showing you, you correct it, and you note the cause. Now they know your number moves only with evidence, both ways.

When the lender's monitor is in the room

The monitor works for the lender, not for you. Do not ask it to take your side, and do not argue with the contractor through it. Say once, early: "Our measurement sheets are available to you after the meeting, and we will copy you on the agreed note." If the monitor's own number differs from yours, that is useful: resolve it with them separately and in writing before the draw goes in. A lender who sees the owner and the monitor reconcile quietly every month trusts the draws, and that trust is worth more than winning any single line.

Afterwards

Send a short written note the same day: certified amount, the basis for each line, the retainage position, the waiver holds and the agreed next steps. Copy the lender's monitor. A written record turns a tense conversation into a fact pattern you can rely on later.

Monthly thread: ethics under payment pressure

Payment is where small corruptions start. A contractor offers to "look after" your representative if the certificate is generous. A subcontractor asks you to sign a waiver it has not earned so a draw can go. Someone suggests certifying a little ahead this month and catching up later. Each looks minor. Each is a false statement in a document a lender, a court or an auditor will rely on.

The rule is simple: the certificate states the facts as measured, every time, and any offer of a benefit linked to a payment decision is declined and reported in writing. A developer whose certificates are known to be honest gets faster draws, cheaper credit and contractors who stop trying.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor, on the certified amount; construction lawyer, on any dispute notice or retention variation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is splitting the difference to keep the peace. Every dollar paid ahead of the work weakens your position at closeout. The control is a measured basis for every line and a written record of every disagreement.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears "our subs are complaining" and pays to protect the subs. If the subs are complaining, the answer is joint cheques and direct verification, not more money to the party not paying them.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile-question pattern: acknowledge, bridge, answer. In this meeting it sounds like: I understand the pressure; the basis is the measurement; here is each line. The same pattern that works with a hostile lender works with a hostile contractor.

Recap

Keep the payment meeting about facts. State the number and its basis, invite correction with evidence, refuse to defer an overbilling, ask the question behind the question, hold retention and waivers by process, and write it down the same day.

Next: Kema on the Week 117 review: six questions, a Red Pen drill and a two-minute boardroom drill on payment.
checklist: I open with the certified number and its basis, then stop.
I invite correction with evidence, the same day if possible.
I never defer an overbilling to next month.
I ask directly whether the contractor has a cash flow problem, then stay silent.
I answer retention requests with the contract position and a written route to terms.
I handle missing waivers by joint cheque or release on receipt, stated as process.
I end the meeting if it stops being about facts, with a time to reconvene.
I send a written summary the same day, copied to the lender's monitor.
head: Field checklist
speak: The payment meeting is a disagreement about facts, so I keep it about facts. I open with our certified number and the basis for each disputed line, then I stop talking. When the contractor pushes, I say that if our measurement is wrong I want to fix it today, and if it is right, it stands. I never say we'll sort it out next month, because that turns an overbilling into a loan. When a contractor overbills hard and asks for early retention release in the same meeting, I ask the question behind the question: is there a cash flow issue I should know about? Then I stay silent. On retention, I state the contract and invite a written proposal that gives the project something in return. Missing waivers mean joint cheques. If the meeting stops being about facts, I end it and reconvene after a joint site walk. And I put everything in writing the same day.
terms: Pencil application — an informal draft of the monthly pay application, agreed in advance so the official one records numbers already checked.
Risk register — the project's list of identified risks, each with an owner, likelihood, impact and response.
Split the difference — settling a factual dispute by meeting halfway, which on a pay application means paying for work that may not exist.

hostile.q: If you don't certify our full application, we'll slow the job down. Is that what you want?
hostile.a: No. I want the job on schedule and you paid promptly for every dollar of work in place. If our measurement is wrong, show me this afternoon and I will correct it. If you slow the work because of a certified payment, I will treat that as a breach and give notice under the contract. Let's walk the three lines now and avoid both.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 117 Review: Pay Applications, Retainage, Waivers and Draws
summary: Six questions test the week's core ideas on construction payment. A Red Pen drill marks up a hypothetical pay application summary with planted defects. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: pay only for measured work, hold some back, prove the money reached the trades, and let the lender's draw follow the same evidence.

Recall

Q. In a pay application meeting, what is the question behind the question when a contractor overbills and asks for early retention release together?

A. Usually, can you help us with our cash? It is a signal of a cash flow problem on this job or across the business, and goes into the risk register.

Q. What is an inspection and test plan?

A. A document listing, for each activity, the inspections and tests required, the acceptance criteria, the records and who must witness or release each step.

Q. What is a temporary works design?

A. The engineered design of structures used only during construction, such as shoring, falsework or excavation support, which must be designed, checked and inspected as seriously as permanent works.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, payment is the one control you will exercise every month of every project. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can run a pay application meeting and defend a draw. Answer each aloud before reading the answer. Then try the Red Pen drill on paper before you read the defects, and time yourself on the boardroom drill.

The six questions

Question 1. What three things does an owner buy with each construction payment?

Answer: Verified work in place, clean title, and a contractor still able to finish.

Question 2. Why does the structure of the schedule of values matter so much?

Answer: Because every application bills against it. Fine lines by trade and area can be measured; coarse lines invite guessing and front-loading, which moves cash ahead of the work.

Question 3. Which waivers should you collect each month, and from whom?

Answer: Conditional waivers for this month's payment and unconditional waivers for last month's, from the contractor and every significant subcontractor and supplier, using statutory forms where the law requires them.

Question 4. Why is retainage a priced term rather than free security?

Answer: Because contractors price the cash they will not receive until completion into their bid. Retainage gives security and leverage at a cost, so it should be set with the bid and released on a defensible schedule.

Question 5. Why does paying the general contractor in full not protect your land on its own?

Answer: Because in many places lien statutes let unpaid subcontractors and suppliers claim against the property directly, regardless of what the owner paid upstream.

Question 6. State Rule 117.

Answer: Never let money owed to the trades, including retention and advance payments, sit unprotected with a party whose balance sheet you have not checked; pay against verified work and track that it reaches the people who did it.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Quincy framed payment as a monthly trade and walked the cycle from pay application to draw. Ford and Cole took the collapse of Carillion in January 2018 as a case of a payment chain that made the trades its lenders. Priya priced retainage, draw lag and lien exposure. LEX explained lien rights, waivers, pay-if-paid and prompt payment, with Canada and Guyana compared in concept. Quincy worked a full pay application and an in-balance check, then ran the meeting where the contractor overbilled.

Red Pen drill

Here is a hypothetical one-paragraph payment summary from a project manager to you. Find the defects before reading on.

Month 9 certificate: 900,000 dollars, being the contractor's claimed percentages on all lines, which look reasonable. Stored transformers at the supplier's yard, 250,000 dollars, included; the supplier confirms they are ours. Retainage reduced to 5 percent from this month as the contractor requested, since we are close to halfway. Unconditional waivers attached for this month's payment. The loan remains in balance because the budget still has 3,000,000 dollars unspent.

The defects. First, the certificate rests on the contractor's percentages, not on measurement. Second, the stored transformers are paid on a supplier's say-so, with no bill of sale, insurance or inspection; title has not been shown. Third, retainage was reduced early on request, without contract basis or anything given in return, and close to halfway is not halfway. Fourth, unconditional waivers for this month's payment are being collected before the money is paid; for unpaid amounts they should be conditional, with unconditional waivers for last month. Fifth, balance is tested on budget remaining rather than an independent cost to complete. Sixth, the phrase "which look reasonable" is a judgement, not a basis; a certificate should say how each line was measured. Six defects in one paragraph, each of which you have seen this week.

Now rewrite the paragraph correctly in your own words. A model: "Month 9 certificate: 702,000 dollars on measured work, line by line, sheets attached. Stored transformers excluded until a bill of sale, insurance and inspection are in place. Retainage held at 10 percent; the step-down applies only at 50 percent measured completion. Conditional waivers attached for this payment and unconditional waivers for last month's, from all major trades. Balance tested against our quantity surveyor's independent cost to complete."

Boardroom drill

Set a timer for two minutes. A potential equity partner asks you: "How do you control payments on a construction job?" Answer aloud, then compare with the model.

The model answer: "We pay only for measured work. The contractor bills monthly against a detailed schedule of values we approved before the first application. Our quantity surveyor walks the site and certifies what is really in place, so time-related lines are paid by elapsed time and stored materials only with title, insurance and inspection. We hold retainage, which we set deliberately with the bid. Every month we collect conditional waivers for this payment and unconditional waivers for the last one, from the contractor and every major trade, and any gap is paid by joint cheque. Our lawyer confirms the local lien and payment law before award. The lender's draw follows the same evidence, and we test balance against an independent cost to complete, not budget remaining. The result is that our money stays behind the work, our title stays clean and we control the closeout."

Score your answer. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you mention measurement, retainage, waivers and the draw? Did you avoid quoting a retention percentage as a standard? Did you finish in two minutes?

Kema's coaching note

If one of the six questions felt slippery, go back to that day's lesson tonight rather than rereading all seven. The waiver question catches most people, because conditional and unconditional sound alike and do opposite things. Say the rule as a sentence you could tell a contractor: conditional for the money I am about to pay, unconditional for the money I already paid. Then record the boardroom drill once more tomorrow morning, before your shift, and listen to both versions. You are listening for one thing above all: whether you said measured work in the first twenty seconds. That phrase is the spine of the whole week.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is signing a certificate you have not checked because the totals add up. The control is to measure, apply the stored materials and waiver conditions, and test balance on cost to complete before any signature.

The beginner's mistake

Treating payment as administration and delegating it entirely. You can delegate the measuring; you cannot delegate the judgment of what you are paying for.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught that contemporaneous records are the evidence that wins disputes. The monthly certificate, the measurement sheets, the waiver log and the same-day meeting note are exactly those records. They will matter again next week, when changes and claims arrive.

Recap

Pay for measured work against an approved schedule of values, hold retainage as a priced term, collect the right waivers from the right people, know the local lien and payment law, and test the draw against an independent cost to complete.

Next: Marco, with Petra, on First Principles: changes and claims, notice, time bars and delay.

head: The six questions
speak: This week came down to one sentence: pay only for measured work, hold some back, prove the money reached the trades, and let the lender's draw follow the same evidence. The contractor bills against a schedule of values I approved, fine enough to measure. My quantity surveyor certifies what is really in place, time-related lines by elapsed time and stored materials only with title. Retainage is security I pay for in the bid, so I set it deliberately and never reduce it early for nothing. I collect conditional waivers for this month and unconditional waivers for last month from every major trade, because lien statutes can let unpaid subcontractors claim against my land even when I paid the contractor. Local counsel confirms the payment law before award. And the lender's draw is tested against an independent cost to complete. Rule 117: never let money owed to the trades sit unprotected with a party whose balance sheet I have not checked.
terms: Certificate for payment — the owner's or architect's statement of the amount properly due for a period, based on measured work.
Bill of sale — a document transferring ownership of goods, used to give the owner title to stored materials before they are installed.
Waiver log — a running record of which parties have delivered which waivers for which payments.

hostile.q: Your project manager's summary says the loan is in balance because budget remains. Is it?
hostile.a: I do not know yet, and that summary is not acceptable. Budget remaining is not cost to complete. I will have our quantity surveyor's independent forecast within two days, tested against the undisbursed loan, and if there is a shortfall, it will come with a plan to fund it. I am also correcting the stored materials and retention errors in the same summary before anything is signed.
